title: Control How Your GPU Shares Work with Green Contexts | NVIDIA Technical Blog
gist: CUDA 13.1 exposes green contexts through the Runtime API, letting a single process carve a GPU's SMs and workqueues into dedicated partitions. On a 148-SM Blackwell GPU, reserving 8 SMs for a latency-critical kernel cut its latency to 0.007 ms versus 0.140 ms with stream priority alone and 3.727 ms with equal priorities, at the cost of fewer SMs for bulk work.

themes.theme: Why intra-GPU partitioning is needed now

insights.claim: GPU applications increasingly run multiple independent components concurrently inside one process (latency-sensitive operators beside throughput kernels, preprocessing beside inference), and these components interfere unpredictably with existing tools.
insights.speaker: Kyrylo Perelygin
insights.so_what: As GPUs grow, single-tenant-per-GPU assumptions break; software-level partitioning becomes a key lever for utilization and latency SLAs.

insights.so_what: NVIDIA is openly repositioning its own legacy abstraction as unfit for large modern GPUs, signaling a programming-model shift toward explicit resource targeting.

insights.claim: Green contexts have existed in the CUDA Driver API since CUDA 12.4, but only from CUDA 13.1 are they accessible through the Runtime API used by most applications.
insights.speaker: Kyrylo Perelygin
insights.so_what: Runtime API exposure moves the feature from niche low-level use toward mainstream framework adoption.

insights.claim: Besides SM partitioning, green contexts can provision workqueues explicitly, because in the traditional model independent stream-ordered workloads may map to the same underlying workqueues and get falsely serialized even when compute is free.
insights.speaker: Kyrylo Perelygin
insights.so_what: Hidden false dependencies in CUDA scheduling are a source of lost utilization that explicit workqueue control can recover.

insights.claim: Green contexts are lightweight to create and destroy and do not implicitly synchronize unrelated GPU work; streams are created from an explicit cudaExecutionContext_t handle instead of hidden thread-local device state.
insights.speaker: Kyrylo Perelygin
insights.so_what: Minimal code change plus explicit targeting lowers adoption friction for frameworks managing multi-stage pipelines.
insights.quote: Instead of relying on hidden thread-local device state, applications explicitly choose a green context and create streams for it.

insights.claim: Green contexts are opt-in and additive: existing applications keep targeting the full device unchanged and can adopt partitions incrementally.
insights.speaker: Kyrylo Perelygin
insights.so_what: Backward compatibility protects CUDA's installed base while extending the moat with finer control features.
insights.quote: Green contexts are opt-in and additive.

insights.claim: On an NVIDIA Blackwell GPU with 148 SMs, a critical kernel running beside a saturating bulk workload had 3.727 ms latency with equal stream priorities, 0.140 ms with high stream priority, and 0.007 ms when given a dedicated 8-SM green context (140 SMs left for bulk).
insights.speaker: Kyrylo Perelygin
insights.so_what: Roughly a 500x latency gap between naive sharing and partitioning shows how much tail latency is left on the table in mixed GPU workloads.

insights.claim: Stream priorities cannot preempt thread blocks already executing on an SM, so a high-priority kernel must still wait for bulk blocks to drain; dedicating SMs removes that wait, costing about a further 20x in latency if omitted.
insights.speaker: Kyrylo Perelygin
insights.so_what: Latency-sensitive inference or comms kernels co-located with training/bulk compute need hard partitioning, not just priority hints.
insights.quote: Stream priorities can’t preempt a block that’s already executing on an SM, so it needs to wait for some of the blocks to drain.

insights.claim: The explicit tradeoff of green-context partitioning is that the bulk workload gets fewer SMs, so the gain in critical-path latency comes from giving up some throughput.
insights.speaker: Kyrylo Perelygin
insights.so_what: Operators must price latency SLAs against throughput loss; partition sizing becomes a tuning knob.
